fields.subhead: Explain how atoms make colored light, and use it to identify elements.

imageSubjects.section: a hydrogen gas discharge tube glowing in a dark lab

slides.notes: Opens 2.5; builds on 2.1 energy levels and delta E. Goal: students leave able to say how an atom makes colored light. IMAGE SLOT EMPTY, photo to shoot or generate: a hydrogen gas discharge tube glowing in a dark lab.

fields.headline:
Where Does Color
Come From?
fields.subhead: Fireworks, neon signs, a flame on a lab burner. Different colors, one question.
fields.keyq: What inside an atom decides the color of the light it gives off?

imageSubjects.concept: a firework burst beside a glowing neon sign, shot at night

slides.notes: Hook. Take two or three answers, do not correct yet; the answer is the section. IMAGE SLOT EMPTY, photo to shoot or generate: a firework burst beside a glowing neon sign, shot at night.

fields.headline: Three Words to Start
fields.subhead: Write these first. The rest of the section uses them.
fields.k1_b: A single packet of light energy.
fields.k2_b: The distance between two wave crests, measured in nm.
fields.mustwrite: A photon is one packet of light. Its energy is set by its wavelength.

imageSubjects.aside: a glass prism splitting white light on a dark bench

slides.notes: Frequency is defined on slide 5 (waves per second). Misconception to catch: 'longer wavelength means more energy'. It is the opposite. IMAGE SLOT EMPTY, photo to shoot or generate: a glass prism splitting white light on a dark bench.

fields.headline: The Visible Spectrum
fields.subhead: Light we can see runs from about 400 nm to 700 nm.
fields.a1_b: One nm is one billionth of a meter: 1 × 10^{−9} m.

slides.notes: Ranges: violet 400-450, blue 450-495, green 495-570, yellow 570-590, orange 590-620, red 620-700 nm (approximate).

fields.headline: Wavelength Sets the Energy
fields.subhead: Shorter wavelength means higher frequency (more waves per second) and more energy per photon.
fields.c1_b:
Red light.
Low frequency.
Low energy per photon.
fields.c2_b:
Violet light.
High frequency.
High energy per photon.
fields.mustwrite: Shorter wavelength means more energy. A violet photon beats a red one.

imageSubjects.concept: a red and a violet laser pointer beam crossing in haze

slides.notes: Defines frequency here: how many waves pass per second. Short wavelength, high frequency, high energy. IMAGE SLOT EMPTY, photo to shoot or generate: a red and a violet laser pointer beam crossing in haze.

fields.headline: The Photon Energy Equation
fields.subhead: Energy goes up as wavelength goes down. Calculator provided.
fields.problem: How much energy does one photon of a given wavelength carry?
fields.q2_b:
E = hc ÷ wavelength
E = h × frequency
c = wavelength × frequency

imageSubjects.setup: a handheld spectroscope resting on a notebook page

slides.notes: FLAG, Matt to confirm: the course sequencing rule delays scientific notation and heavy math (courses/chemistry/DECISIONS.md, Course sequencing rules). This deck holds to ONE student calculation, calculator provided, 3 sig figs. If you prefer S2.5 conceptual only, defer the calculation. Constants: h = 6.626e-34 J s, c = 3.00e8 m/s. Equations are for reference; students use only E = hc / wavelength today. IMAGE SLOT EMPTY, photo to shoot or generate: a handheld spectroscope resting on a notebook page.

fields.headline: Hot Solid or Hot Gas
fields.subhead: What is glowing decides what the spectrum looks like.
fields.c1_b:
A glowing filament.

Gives every color, no gaps.
fields.c2_b:
Excited atoms in a tube.

Give a few separate lines.
fields.mustwrite: A hot solid gives a continuous spectrum. A hot gas gives a line spectrum.

imageSubjects.concept: an incandescent bulb filament beside a lit neon tube

slides.notes: Hot solid gives all colors; hot gas gives separate lines. LED and fluorescence are out of scope. IMAGE SLOT EMPTY, photo to shoot or generate: an incandescent bulb filament beside a lit neon tube.

fields.headline: Three Kinds of Spectra
fields.subhead: Same range of colors, three different patterns.
fields.a1_b: Every color, no gaps. Made by a hot solid.
fields.a2_b: Bright lines on black. Made by a hot gas.
fields.a3_b: Dark lines at the same places as emission lines.

slides.notes: Absorption lines sit at the same wavelengths as the element's emission lines. Absorption in starlight reveals composition.

fields.headline: Hydrogen's Visible Emission Spectrum
fields.subhead: Four lines, computed from the energy levels.
fields.a2_b: Every one is a drop that ends at n = 2.
fields.a3_b: More sit in the ultraviolet (UV) and infrared (IR). Your eyes miss them.

slides.notes: Lines are 656, 486, 434, 410 nm, all ending at n = 2. Hydrogen has more lines in the UV (2 to 1 is about 122 nm) and IR (4 to 3 is about 1876 nm). Misconception: 'hydrogen has only four lines'.

fields.headline: Which Drop Makes Which Line
fields.subhead: Each line is one electron dropping to n = 2.
fields.a1_b: Heat or electricity lifts an electron up a level.
fields.a2_b: The drop releases one photon with energy ΔE.
fields.a3_b: More energy, shorter wavelength, bluer light.

slides.notes: Each line is one drop to n = 2. Electrons drop to lower levels; they do not fall into the nucleus.

fields.headline: Example: Color of the 3 to 2 Drop
fields.subhead: Calculator provided. Copy the setup, not just the answer.
fields.problem: Hydrogen's 3 to 2 drop emits a 3.03 × 10^{−19} J photon. Find its wavelength and color.

imageSubjects.aside: a hydrogen discharge tube glowing pink-magenta

slides.notes: FLAG, Matt to confirm: the course sequencing rule delays scientific notation and heavy math (courses/chemistry/DECISIONS.md, Course sequencing rules). This deck holds to ONE student calculation, calculator provided, 3 sig figs. If you prefer S2.5 conceptual only, defer the calculation. Delta E for 3 to 2 comes from S2.1 (3.03e-19 J). OPTIONAL Example 2 (dropped from this deck): the 486 nm line is the 4 to 2 drop. Check: delta E = 2.18e-18 x (1/4 - 1/16) = 4.09e-19 J; wavelength = 1.988e-25 / 4.09e-19 = 4.86e-7 m = 486 nm, blue-green. Re-derived for this revision. fields.headline: The 3 to 2 Drop, Worked
fields.subhead: Rearrange, divide, then convert meters to nanometers.
fields.mustwrite: 656 nm is red: the 3 to 2 drop makes hydrogen's red line.

fields.headline: Four Drops to n = 2
fields.subhead: A pre-built table. Read it, do not recalculate it.
fields.a1_b: Bigger drop: more energy, shorter wavelength.
fields.a2_b: The first row is the example you just solved.
fields.a3_b: Joules, for one photon from one atom.

slides.notes: Pre-built table, read-only; check values against the example. 3 to 2: 3.03e-19 J, 656 nm; 4 to 2: 4.09e-19 J, 486 nm; 5 to 2: 4.58e-19 J, 434 nm; 6 to 2: 4.84e-19 J, 410 nm. Scientific-notation flag applies here too (see slide 6).

fields.headline: Every Element Has Its Own Lines
fields.subhead: Only certain energy drops exist, so only certain lines appear.
fields.c1_b:
Each element has its own energy levels.

So its drops, and its lines, are its own.
fields.c2_b:
Line positions identify an element.

Helium was first found in sunlight, 1868.
fields.mustwrite: Each element has a unique line spectrum because its energy levels are unique.

imageSubjects.concept: line spectra of several gas discharge tubes side by side, photographed through a spectroscope

slides.notes: Helium was first detected in the Sun's spectrum, 1868 (Janssen and Lockyer). Line positions identify an element. IMAGE SLOT EMPTY, photo to shoot or generate: line spectra of several gas discharge tubes side by side, photographed through a spectroscope.

fields.headline:
Same Idea,
In a Flame
fields.subhead: Metal ions in a flame emit light too. The color helps you identify the metal.

imageSubjects.divider: a lab burner flame with a wire loop of metal salt, shot in a darkened room

fields.headline: How a Flame Test Makes Color
fields.subhead: The color is not the metal burning. It is electrons dropping levels.
fields.c1_b: Heat lifts electrons in the metal ion to higher levels.
fields.c2_b: They release photons of visible light. The color helps identify the metal.
fields.mustwrite: The color of the emitted light helps identify the metal ion.

imageSubjects.concept: a flame test photograph, a bright lilac flame from a wire loop

slides.notes: PROVISIONAL (flame section): flame tests are not a confirmed U2 lab (DECISIONS.md open question 4), so this is science only, no procedure. PROVISIONAL: Ca, Sr, Ba and Cu flame colors come largely from molecular emitters (such as CaOH, SrOH, BaOH, CuCl), not single atomic lines; the electron-drop explanation is a valid HS simplification. Flame photos still to be shot. Color claims checked against textbook convention only. The color suggests the ion; it does not prove it. IMAGE SLOT EMPTY, photo to shoot or generate: a flame test photograph, a bright lilac flame from a wire loop.

fields.headline: Flame Test Colors, Part 1
fields.subhead: Compare the color you see to the table.
fields.a1_b: Each metal ion has a typical flame color.
fields.a2_b: A little Na^{+} can turn a flame yellow.
fields.a3_b: A flame color is a mix, not one exact line.

slides.notes: PROVISIONAL (flame section): flame tests are not a confirmed U2 lab (DECISIONS.md open question 4), so this is science only, no procedure. PROVISIONAL: colors are textbook convention only; swatches are illustrations, not photographs, and flame photos are still to be shot. Do not state a color is one exact wavelength. K lilac is often masked by sodium; the cobalt-glass technique is lab procedure and is not in scope.

fields.headline: Flame Test Colors, Part 2
fields.subhead: Some of these colors look a lot alike.
fields.a1_b: Sr^{2+} red and Ca^{2+} orange-red are easy to confuse.
fields.a2_b: Many elements give no flame color we can see.
fields.a3_b: It narrows the options. It does not prove the ion.

slides.notes: PROVISIONAL (flame section): flame tests are not a confirmed U2 lab (DECISIONS.md open question 4), so this is science only, no procedure. PROVISIONAL: textbook colors only, Ca, Sr, Ba, Cu largely molecular emitters; photos still to be shot. Many elements give no visible flame color.

fields.headline: Example: Identify the Metals
fields.subhead: Use the flame color tables. Copy the reasoning.
fields.problem: One salt burns lilac with a trace of yellow. Another burns orange-red. Which metals?
fields.g1_b:
Salt A: lilac, with some yellow
Salt B: orange-red
fields.g2_b: The metal ion behind each color
fields.mustwrite: Write the metal ion for each color, not just the color.

fields.headline: Two Unknowns, Identified
fields.subhead: Sodium is a common contaminant.
fields.f1_b:
Match each color
to the table.
Na^{+} gives yellow.
fields.work:
Salt A: K^{+} (lilac)
Yellow trace: Na^{+}
Salt B: Ca^{2+} (orange-red)
Sr^{2+} looks similar
fields.mustwrite: Flame colors can look alike, so a flame test alone does not prove the ion.

fields.k1_b: Which has more energy, a red photon or a blue photon? Why?
fields.k2_b: Why does each element have its own line spectrum?

slides.notes: Formative check. OPTIONAL extra item 3 (dropped from this deck): calculate the wavelength of a 4.58e-19 J photon (5 to 2 in hydrogen) and state the color. Answer: wavelength = 1.988e-25 / 4.58e-19 = 4.34e-7 m = 434 nm, blue-violet. Check: delta E = 2.18e-18 x (1/4 - 1/25) = 4.58e-19 J. Re-derived for this revision. Answers to the three on-slide items: blue (shorter wavelength, more energy); each element has unique energy levels so unique photon energies; lilac suggests K+ (heat lifts electrons, they drop, photons of visible light).
